Prealgebra · Lesson 10.2

The Multiplication Principle

Solve this lesson →All lessons

Last lesson we counted by adding and subtracting whole piles of items. Now we count outcomes that get built up in steps, like an outfit picked one piece at a time, where each step has its own set of options.

Problem
You have 55 shirts and 44 pairs of pants. How many different shirt-and-pants outfits can you make?
Show a hint
  • Pick just one shirt for a moment and hold it still. With that single shirt in your hand, how many different outfits can you build by trying each of the 44 pairs of pants with it?
  • One shirt gives 44 outfits. Now you have 55 shirts, and every shirt gets its own group of 44 outfits, with no outfit ever shared between two shirts. So you are stacking up 55 groups that each hold 44 outfits.
  • You have 55 equal groups of 44 outfits, so add 4+4+4+4+44+4+4+4+4, which is the same as the product 5×45×4.
Show the full solution
Hold one shirt still. It pairs with each of the 44 pairs of pants, so that single shirt gives 44 outfits. Every one of the 55 shirts gives its own 44, and none of those repeat, so the total is 5×4=205×4=20​. Equal-sized groups get multiplied, which beats adding 4+4+4+4+44+4+4+4+4 by hand.
Problem
A game lets you pick one of 22 body types, 33 hair styles, 44 outfits, and 66 weapons. How many different heroes can you build?
Show a hint
  • Building a hero is four separate decisions in a row, one for each menu, so set up four slots and write the number of choices that fit in each one.
  • When a job is made of stages done one after another, and the choices at each stage do not change the choices at the next, you multiply the slot numbers together instead of adding them.
  • Your four slots hold 22, 33, 44, and 66, so multiply 2×3×4×62×3×4×6 to get the total.
Show the full solution
Four menus means four slots, holding 22, 33, 44, and 66 choices. Multiply straight across. 2×3=62×3=6, then 6×4=246×4=24, then 24×6=14424×6=144, so you can build 144144​ heroes. Picking a body type does not remove any hair or outfit options, so every stage keeps its full count and the slots multiply.
Problem
A lock has 33 dials, each showing one of 66 colored symbols. Repeats are allowed. How many 33-symbol codes are possible?
Show a hint
  • Picture the lock as 33 slots side by side. For each slot, ask how many symbols could go there. Since a symbol can repeat, choosing it for one dial does not stop you from using it again on the next.
  • Use the multiplication principle. Count the choices for the first dial, then the second, then the third, and multiply those counts together to get the total number of codes.
  • Each dial has 66 choices, and the choices stay the same because repeats are allowed. So the total is 6×6×66×6×6. Work out that product.
Show the full solution
Each of the 33 dials can show any of the 66 symbols, so multiply 6×6×6=63=2166×6×6=63=216. The lock has 216216​ codes. Repeats being allowed is what keeps the count at 66 every time, since using a symbol on one dial does not use it up.
Key idea
The Multiplication Principle. When a task is built from independent stages, the total number of ways is the product of the per-stage counts. So aa ways for the first stage and bb ways for the second give a×ba×b in all. Every problem in this lesson uses the same slot-and-box method. Draw one box for each stage, write inside it how many options that stage has, and multiply straight across. Each choice still leaves a full set of choices at the next stage, so the counts multiply rather than add.
Problem
A license plate is 2 letters then 2 digits. Repeats allowed. How many different plates are possible?
Show a hint
  • Picture the plate as four empty slots in a row, two for letters and two for digits. Each slot gets filled on its own, so think about how many choices live in each one.
  • Use the multiplication principle. Count the choices for each slot separately, then multiply all four counts together. Because repeats are allowed, a slot does not lose any choices from the slots before it.
  • A letter slot has 2626 choices and a digit slot has 1010 choices, so the count is 26×26×10×1026×26×10×10. Multiply these to finish.
Show the full solution
Four slots, letter, letter, digit, digit. A letter slot has 2626 choices and a digit slot has 1010, and repeats are allowed so no slot loses anything to the ones before it. The two letters give 26×26=67626×26=676, the two digits give 10×10=10010×10=100, and 676×100=67600676×100=67600. There are 6760067600​ plates.
Problem
How many different orders can 66 different books be arranged on a shelf?
Show a hint
  • Picture the shelf as 66 empty slots in a row, one for each spot from left to right. Filling the slots one at a time is far easier than trying to list every arrangement by hand.
  • Use the slot-and-box habit. Count the choices for the first slot, then the second, and so on, and multiply all the counts together. The key is that once a book is placed it is gone, so each slot has one fewer choice than the slot before it.
  • The first slot has 66 books to choose from, the next has 55 left, then 44, then 33, then 22, and the last slot has just 11 book remaining, so multiply 6×5×4×3×2×16×5×4×3×2×1.
Show the full solution
Fill 66 shelf slots left to right. The first slot has 66 books to choose from, then 55 are left, then 44, 33, 22, and 11. Multiply, 6×5×4×3×2×1=720,6×5×4×3×2×1=720, so there are 720720​ orders. Placing a book uses it up, so each slot has one fewer choice than the last. That countdown product is 6!6!.
Key idea
Repeats or no repeats. When repeats are allowed, using an option in one box does not remove it from the rest, so every box has kk options and nn boxes give knkn. When repeats are not allowed, each option used is unavailable later, so the counts drop by one at each box, k,k−1,k−2,…k,k−1,k−2,…. Arranging all nn different things in a row continues down to 11, giving n×(n−1)×⋯×1=n!n×(n−1)×⋯×1=n!, called nn factorial.
Problem
99 club members compete for president, vice president, and treasurer. Nobody holds two jobs. How many ways can the three jobs be filled?
Show a hint
  • Think of three empty boxes in a row, one for president, one for vice president, and one for treasurer. You are filling them one at a time from the 99 members, and someone who takes a job cannot be picked again.
  • Count the choices for each box in turn. Any of the 99 members could be president. Once that person is chosen, only 88 people are left to be vice president, and after that only 77 are left to be treasurer. Then multiply the box counts together.
  • You only have three boxes, so you stop after three steps and multiply 9×8×79×8×7.
Show the full solution
Any of the 99 members could be president. That leaves 88 people for vice president and 77 for treasurer, so multiply 9×8×79×8×7. Since 9×8=729×8=72 and 72×7=50472×7=504, the jobs can be filled in 504504​ ways. Three jobs means three factors, so stop the countdown after three instead of running it down to 11.
Key idea
Partial arrangement. To fill rr slots from nn items in order with no repeats, take exactly rr descending factors. Write n×(n−1)×(n−2)×⋯n×(n−1)×(n−2)×⋯ for rr factors, then stop. Each new box drops the count by one, since one more item is already placed and cannot be reused. A full arrangement would run down to 11 and give n!n!, so check that you have rr factors for rr slots.
Problem
There are 900900 three-digit numbers. How many of them do NOT have all three digits the same?
Show a hint
  • Instead of chasing the huge pile of numbers you want, try counting the tiny pile you do not want first. How many 33-digit numbers have all three digits the same?
  • This is the total-minus-bad move from 10.110.1. Count every 33-digit number that is all the same digit, then take that count away from the 900900. The ones left over are the numbers that do NOT have all three digits the same.
  • The all-same numbers are 111,222,333,444,555,666,777,888,999111,222,333,444,555,666,777,888,999, which is 99 of them. Now do 900−9900−9.
Show the full solution
Count the ones you do not want. The 33-digit numbers with all three digits the same are 111,222,333,444,555,666,777,888,999111,222,333,444,555,666,777,888,999, which is 99 of them. Take those from the 900900 and you get 900−9=891900−9=891​. Every three-digit number is either all-same or not, so subtracting the small group leaves exactly the big one. That is the total-minus-bad move from 10.110.1.
Problem
How many three-digit numbers are there? (The leading digit cannot be 00.)
Show a hint
  • Draw three empty boxes, one for the hundreds digit, one for the tens digit, and one for the units digit. Then ask how many digits are allowed in each box, and notice that the boxes will not all have the same number of choices.
  • Fill the tightest box first. The hundreds digit may be anything except 00, so count those choices carefully. The other two boxes have no rule at all, so each can be any digit from 00 to 99. Once you know the choices in each box, the multiplication principle says you multiply them together.
  • The hundreds box has 99 choices, the tens box has 1010, and the units box has 1010, so you are working out 9×10×109×10×10.
Show the full solution
Three boxes, hundreds, tens, units. The hundreds box cannot be 00, so it has the 99 choices 11 through 99, and the tens and units boxes each take any of 1010 digits. Multiply, 9×10×10=900,9×10×10=900, so there are 900900​ three-digit numbers. Total minus bad gets there too. All 10×10×10=100010×10×10=1000 digit strings minus the 100100 that start with 00 is 900900.
Problem
A 4-digit palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards, and the leading digit is not 00. How many 4-digit palindromes are there?
Show a hint
  • Draw four slots for the four digits. A palindrome forces some of them to copy others, so you do not really get to choose all four. Which slots are you actually free to pick?
  • Only the first digit and the second digit are free choices. Once you pick them, the third digit must copy the second and the fourth must copy the first. So count the ways to fill just those two free slots and multiply.
  • The first digit has 99 choices (it cannot be 00), and the second digit has 1010 choices (any of 00 through 99). The last two are forced. Multiply 9×109×10 to finish.
Show the full solution
Only the first two digits are free, since the third has to copy the second and the fourth has to copy the first. The first digit has 99 choices because it cannot be 00, and the second has 1010. Multiply, 9×10=909×10=90, so there are 9090​ four-digit palindromes. A forced slot has 11 way, so it contributes a factor of 11 and never changes the product.
Problem
Six people line up. The tallest must stand at the far left and the shortest at the far right. How many orders for the whole row are possible?
Show a hint
  • Two of the six spots are already decided for you. The far left end has to be the tallest person and the far right end has to be the shortest person, so those two spots have no choices left. The only real question is what happens in the four spots in the middle.
  • Pin down the forced ends first and then forget about them. That leaves four people who still need places and exactly four open middle spots, and every one of those people is different. So you are just arranging four distinct people in four spots in a row.
  • Fill the four middle spots one at a time. The first open spot has 44 people who could go there, then 33 left for the next, then 22, then 11. Multiply those together, which is 4×3×2×1=4!4×3×2×1=4!, and that is your count.
Show the full solution
The two ends are forced, the tallest on the left and the shortest on the right, so each end has 11 way. That leaves 44 people for the 44 middle spots, and those fill in 4×3×2×1=244×3×2×1=24 ways. The whole row has 2424​ orders. Pinning down the forced spots first turns a six-person lineup into a plain arrangement of four.
Key idea
Restrictions, two methods. When a count comes with a rule, two methods give the same answer. First method, fill the restricted box first. Count the choices there, like a leading digit with only 99 choices instead of 1010, then multiply by the choices left in the other boxes. Second method, count every outcome as if there were no rule, then subtract the ones that break the rule, the total minus bad count from 10.1. Use whichever method is shorter.
Fun fact
In 1808 Christian Kramp introduced the ! symbol so that 5×4×3×2×15×4×3×2×1 could be written as 5!5!. One mark replaced the entire descending product.
Problem
A 44-digit PIN has an odd first digit, an even second digit (including 00), and all four digits distinct. How many PINs follow all three rules?
Show a hint
  • Draw four empty boxes, one for each digit, and fill them left to right. Settle the digit with the strictest rule first, then move along, and remember that once a digit is used it cannot show up again.
  • The first box must be odd, so count how many odd digits there are from 00 to 99. The second box must be even, so count the even digits. After that the third and fourth boxes can be any leftover digit, so subtract the ones already taken.
  • You should have 55 odd choices for the first box and 55 even choices for the second. The third box is any digit except the two already used, which leaves 88, and the fourth box leaves 77. Multiply all four counts together.
Show the full solution
The first digit must be odd, so it is one of 1,3,5,7,91,3,5,7,9, giving 55 choices. The second must be even, one of 0,2,4,6,80,2,4,6,8, another 55. The third digit has to dodge the 22 digits already used, leaving 88, and the fourth dodges 33, leaving 77. Multiply, 5×5×8×7=1400,5×5×8×7=1400, so 14001400​ PINs work. Odd and even digits never overlap, so the second box keeps all 55 of its choices.
Problem
A locker tag is one letter then three distinct digits, and the first digit cannot be 00. How many different tags are possible?
Show a hint
  • Picture the tag as four boxes in a row, one for the letter and three for the digits. The slot-and-box habit lets you count one box at a time and then multiply.
  • Fill the boxes left to right and count the choices for each, but watch the two catches. The first digit cannot be 00, and every later digit has to dodge the digits you already used.
  • The letter has 2626 choices. The first digit has 99 choices since 00 is banned. The second digit has 99 choices, any of the 1010 digits except the one already placed. The third digit has 88 choices. Now find 26×9×9×826×9×9×8.
Show the full solution
The letter box has 2626 choices. The first digit cannot be 00, so it has 99. The second digit can be any digit except the one already used, so 99 again, and the third must dodge both, leaving 88. Multiply, 26×9=23426×9=234, then 234×9=2106234×9=2106, then 2106×8=168482106×8=16848. There are 1684816848​ tags. Two different restrictions can land on the same box count for different reasons.

Practice these ideas

Practice
You have 33 hats and 66 scarves. How many different hat-and-scarf pairs can you make?
Show the solution
One hat pairs with each of the 66 scarves, so that hat alone gives 66 pairs. All 33 hats give three groups of 66 with no overlap, so 3×6=183×6=18​ pairs.
Practice
An ice cream stand has 55 cone types and 55 flavors (22 fruit and 33 chocolate). How many different cones can you order?
Show the solution
There are 2+3=52+3=5 flavors in all. Each of the 55 cone types pairs with each flavor, so 5×5=255×5=25​ cones. The flavors arrive in two groups, so add those together first, then multiply across the two stages.
Practice
A breakfast combo is one drink, one main, and one fruit: 22 drinks, 55 mains, 33 fruits. How many different combos are possible?
Show the solution
Multiply the options at each step, 22 drinks, 55 mains, 33 fruits. The first two steps give 2×5=102×5=10 drink-and-main pairs, and each of those takes any of 33 fruits, so 10×3=3010×3=30​ combos.
Practice
A signal has 33 lights, each glowing in one of 44 colors. Repeats allowed. How many different signals are possible?
Show the solution
Repeats are allowed, so each of the 33 lights has all 44 colors open to it. Multiply, 4×4×4=43=644×4×4=43=64​ signals. The first light's color does not use anything up, which is why the count stays at 44 every time.
Practice
How many 44-digit numbers are there? (The leading digit cannot be 00.)
Show the solution
The leading slot cannot be 00, so it has the 99 choices 11 through 99. The other three slots each take any digit from 00 to 99, so 1010 choices each. Multiply, 9×10×10×10=9000,9×10×10×10=9000, so there are 90009000​ four-digit numbers.
Practice
How many different orders can 55 different trophies be arranged on a shelf?
Show the solution
Fill the five spots left to right. The first has 55 trophies to choose from, then 44 are left, then 33, then 22, then 11. Multiply, 5×4×3×2×1=1205×4×3×2×1=120, so there are 120120​ orders. Each trophy placed is used up, and that countdown to 11 is exactly what 5!5! means.
Practice
A race has 88 runners. The fastest gets gold and the next gets silver. How many ways can the two medals be awarded?
Show the solution
Think of two spots to fill in order, the gold first and then the silver. For the gold, any of the 88 runners could finish first, so there are 88 choices. Once the gold is decided, that runner is taken, which leaves 77 runners who could come in second for the silver. The multiplication principle says you multiply the number of choices for each spot, and you get 8×7=56.8×7=56. So the two medals can be awarded in 5656​ different ways.
Practice
A tag has 22 characters from 99 symbols. Repeats are allowed, but the two characters cannot match. How many tags are possible?
Show the solution
The left spot takes any of the 99 symbols. The right spot can be anything except the symbol you just placed, so 88 are still allowed. Multiply, 9×8=729×8=72​ tags. Repeats are allowed in general, and the matching rule bans exactly one symbol on the right, so the count drops by just 11.
Practice
Four paintings hang in a row. One special painting is fixed in the far left spot. How many different orders for the whole row are possible?
Show the solution
The star painting is locked into the far left spot, so only the other three move. Fill the three open spots one at a time with 33, then 22, then 11 choices, which gives 3×2×1=63×2×1=6​ orders. A locked spot has 11 way, so it contributes a factor of 11 and drops out of the product.
Practice
A 4-digit palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards, and no digit may be 00. How many such palindromes are there?
Show the solution
A 4-digit palindrome has the pattern ABBAABBA, so only the first two digits are free. No digit may be 00, so each free digit is one of 11 through 99, which is 99 choices. Multiply, 9×9=819×9=81​ palindromes. The last two digits are copies, so each contributes a factor of 11.
Practice
There are 900900 three-digit numbers, and exactly 9090 of them are palindromes. How many three-digit numbers are NOT palindromes?
Show the solution
It is easier to count the ones we do not want and take them away. There are 900900 three-digit numbers in total, and 9090 of them are palindromes. So the numbers that are not palindromes are everything else, which gives 900−90=810900−90=810. So the answer is 810810​.
Practice
There are 33 roads from A to B and 44 roads from B to C. How many different routes are there from A to C?
Show the solution
Pick a road from A to B in 33 ways, then a road from B to C in 44 ways. Every first road opens all 44 ways to finish, so multiply, 3×4=123×4=12​ routes.
Practice
A pizza has one each of: 22 crusts, 22 sauces, 33 cheeses, 44 toppings. How many different pizzas can you build?
Show the solution
Multiply the options at each step, 22 crusts, 22 sauces, 33 cheeses, 44 toppings. Left to right, 2×2=42×2=4, then 4×3=124×3=12, then 12×4=4812×4=48, so there are 4848​ pizzas.
Practice
A locker code is 22 distinct letters then 22 distinct digits. How many different codes are possible?
Show the solution
The first letter has 2626 choices and the second must differ, leaving 2525, so the letters give 26×25=65026×25=650. The first digit has 1010 choices and the second 99, so the digits give 9090. Then 650×90=58500650×90=58500​ codes. Making a pair distinct only trims the second slot by one, and everything still multiplies.
